units.title: Paper 1 and 2: 1 Imperialism and the emergence of world powers, c.1870-1918

topics.title: 1.1 Why was imperialism a significant force in Africa from 1870?

outcomes.text: Explain the economic, religious-cultural and rivalry motives for the Scramble for Africa.
Compare direct and indirect rule in the colonies.
Describe the activities of explorers Barth, Livingstone and Stanley.
Explain how technology and the Suez Canal helped colonisation.
Explain the effects of arbitrary boundaries imposed by colonial powers.
Explain human exploitation and abuse in the Belgian Congo.
Assess the colonial spread of Christianity, healthcare, education and infrastructure.
Explain the causes and impact of African resistance: the Anglo-Zulu War, Ndebele rebellion, Adwa and the Herero War.

topics.title: 1.2 What was the impact of imperial expansion on international relations?

outcomes.text: Explain the purpose of the Berlin Conference, including Bismarck's pressures and the powers' intentions.
Explain its outcomes: effective occupation, Leopold's Congo, ending slavery and free trade.

subtopics.title: Colonial rivalries and attempts to ease them

outcomes.text: Explain rivalries: Britain and Germany, France and Britain at Fashoda, France and Germany over Morocco.
Explain the end of splendid isolation and the Anglo-French Entente.
Explain the Algeciras conference and the 1911 convention ending the Agadir crisis.
Describe the extent of empires in 1914, their influence on alliances and contemporary verdicts.

topics.title: 1.3 Why did Japan emerge as a world power?

outcomes.text: Explain Japan's relations with western powers: Perry's mission and the unequal treaties.
Explain the reasons for rapid modernisation: Meiji Restoration, industry, western technology and education.
Explain recognition as a world power: relations with Korea, the 1902 Anglo-Japanese Treaty and the Russo-Japanese War.
Describe Japan's role in the First World War, seizure of German Pacific possessions and Russian intervention.

topics.title: 1.4 Why did the USA emerge as a world power?

outcomes.text: Explain changing attitudes to overseas expansion: the closing frontier, Mahan, the Great White Fleet.
Explain rapid economic growth, the Panic of 1893 and the Panama Canal.
Explain the reasons for and impact of the Spanish-American War, including yellow journalism and the Maine.
Explain the Philippine-American War, US motives and Filipino resistance.

subtopics.title: US entry into the First World War

outcomes.text: Explain US relations with Germany, Britain and France.
Explain Wilson's policy, anti-war groups, U-boats and the Lusitania.
Explain the Zimmermann telegram and the impact of US intervention.

units.title: Paper 1 and 2: 2 International relations 1919-29: conflict and cooperation

topics.title: 2.1 Why was there such extensive dissatisfaction with the peace settlements of 1919-20?

outcomes.text: Explain the aims of the Big Three and the representation of other powers at Versailles.
Describe the key terms of the Treaties of Versailles, Trianon, Neuilly, Saint Germain and Sevres.
Explain difficulties from new boundaries and inconsistent self-determination.
Explain reactions of the victors, the defeated and Russia.
Explain the reparations issue: war guilt, size and payment.

topics.title: 2.2 Why was the League of Nations created and what challenges did it face in the 1920s?

outcomes.text: Explain the creation of the League: Wilson's 14 points, the treaties, aims and structure.
Explain its weaknesses: restricted membership, leadership, voting and enforcement.
Explain collective security and the League's handling of Aaland, Teschen, Vilna, Upper Silesia, Memel and Greco-Bulgarian disputes.
Explain the role of the refugee, ILO, slavery, disarmament and mandates bodies.

topics.title: 2.3 How and why did international tensions remain high after the Versailles settlement?

outcomes.text: Explain crises: Fiume, Corfu, the Ruhr, German hyperinflation and successor-state problems.
Explain the aims and impact of the Little Entente, Washington, Genoa, Rapallo and Lausanne.
Explain changing relations between European powers, the Soviet Union, the USA and Japan.

topics.title: 2.4 How and why did international relations improve, 1924-29?

outcomes.text: Explain the Dawes Plan, Stresemann, German entry to the League and the Young Plan.
Explain the Geneva Protocol, Locarno, the Kellogg-Briand Pact and the 1929 Hague Conference.
Explain France-Germany relations, Mussolini's ambitions and shifting relations with the Soviet Union.
Judge whether improved relations were reality or illusion, including the Wall Street Crash.

units.title: Paper 1 and 2: 3 International history 1929-39: the rise of extremism and the road to war

topics.title: 3.1 How did the rise of extremism affect international relations?

outcomes.text: Explain how the Depression affected politics in Germany, Japan, Italy and the USA.
Explain the failure of the World Disarmament Conference, 1932-34.
Explain the London Naval Conference, Stresa Front, Rome-Berlin Axis and Anti-Comintern Pact.
Explain the Soviet response to Nazism, Comintern and fear of Communism.

topics.title: 3.2 Why did the League of Nations fail to keep the peace in the 1930s?

outcomes.text: Explain the League's response to Manchuria and Abyssinia.
Explain withdrawals, the admission of the USSR and talks outside the League.
Explain the responses to the Spanish Civil War and the failure of non-intervention.
Explain the causes of the League's failure: disarmament, absent powers, reliance on Britain and France, Depression, nationalism.

topics.title: 3.3 Why, and with what effects, did Britain and France pursue appeasement?

outcomes.text: Explain British pressures: the Depression, 10-year rule, King and Country debate and Peace Ballot.
Explain sympathy for Nazi policy and fascism as a bulwark against Bolshevism.
Explain French economic and political problems, communism, the 1936 election and the Maginot Line.
Explain the responses to rearmament, the Naval Agreement and the Rhineland.
Explain acceptance of the Anschluss, the Sudetenland crisis and Munich.
Explain responses to the occupation of Prague.
Assess the successes and failures of appeasement.

topics.title: 3.4 Why did war break out in 1939?

outcomes.text: Explain Hitler's underlying aims and the steps from rearmament to Czechoslovakia.
Explain British rearmament: aircraft, air raid preparation and 1939 targets.
Explain German alliances: Anti-Comintern Pact, Pact of Steel and Nazi-Soviet Pact.
Explain German-Polish issues: Danzig and the Polish Corridor.
Explain the end of appeasement and the Anglo-French guarantee.
Explain Hitler's disagreement with the High Command and his intentions.

topics.title: Interpreting the Holocaust

outcomes.text: Explain why historians produce different interpretations: evidence, selection, time and place.
Explain how historians' questions, ideology and approaches differ.
Assess whether the Holocaust grew from racist ideas that pre-dated the Nazis.
Explain intentionalism and the role of Hitler's planning.
Explain structuralism and the Nazi state.
Explain functionalism and the role of war.
Explain synthesis interpretations.
Debate who carried out the Holocaust and why, including non-Germans.
Debate Jewish resistance and whether victims beyond Jews should be included.
Explain the response of the USA and Britain at the time.

units.title: Paper 4: 1 The Soviet Empire in Eastern Europe, 1953-91

topics.title: 1.1 How did the Soviet relationship with the satellite states develop up to 1968?

outcomes.text: Explain the formation of the Warsaw Pact and the reasons for it.
Describe government in Czechoslovakia, Poland, East Germany and Hungary.
Explain repression: censorship, the Stasi, Church policy and emigration limits.
Explain economic centralisation and changing living standards.
Explain the 1950s uprisings in Poland and East Germany.
Explain the causes, course and impact of the Hungarian uprising.
Explain the Berlin problem and the building of the Wall.
Explain the Prague Spring and Soviet reactions including the Brezhnev Doctrine.

topics.title: 1.2 Why did 1964-85 become characterised by political and economic stagnation?

outcomes.text: Explain Brezhnev's aims, Andropov and Chernenko.
Explain corruption, the nomenklatura and gerontocracy.
Explain the Soviet economy's problems: reform attempts, defence spending and stagnation.
Explain detente, the Afghanistan invasion and the Second Cold War.
Describe developments, economic reforms and social policies in the satellite states.
Explain challenges to Soviet control: Western influence, activism and the Church.

topics.title: 1.3 How did Gorbachev try to respond to the crisis in the Soviet Union?

outcomes.text: Explain the reasons for Gorbachev's rise and his changes.
Describe the 1985 situation: economy, shortages, deficit, absenteeism and conditions.
Explain pressures for change within and outside the USSR.
Explain 'new thinking': glasnost, perestroika and demokratizatsiya.
Explain economic restructuring: the 12th Five Year Plan, fragmentation, declining trade and Chernobyl.
Explain the impact on relations with the USA, including the summits.

topics.title: 1.4 How and why did Soviet control of Eastern Europe collapse in 1991?

outcomes.text: Explain the growth of Solidarity and Poland's economic problems.
Describe the Gdansk events of August 1980 and the 21 Demands.
Explain the reactions of the Polish government, the USSR and martial law.
Explain nationalist movements, dissent and Soviet reactions in Kazakhstan and the Baltic states.
Explain the Sinatra Doctrine, re-legalising Solidarity and the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Explain opposition to Gorbachev, the 1991 coup and his resignation.
Explain the collapse of Soviet control in the republics.

units.title: Paper 4: 2 End of minority rule in South Africa and Zimbabwe, 1948-94

topics.title: 2.1 How was the apartheid state established and what was its impact, 1948-59?

outcomes.text: Describe South Africa c.1948: mining, manufacturing, agriculture and the lives of Black South Africans.
Explain the National Party's 1948 victory: war, Afrikaner nationalism, Smuts and the electoral system.
Explain apartheid laws, the pass system, Bantustans and Black education.
Explain how these measures changed everyday life.
Explain the roles of the ANC and PAC.
Explain the Defiance Campaign and the 1956 anti-pass march.
Explain the Freedom Charter, government suppression and the Treason Trials.

topics.title: 2.2 How did resistance grow and how did the authorities respond, 1960-77?

outcomes.text: Explain the ANC, PAC and the Year of the Pass, Sharpeville and Langa.
Explain Mandela, Umkhonto we Sizwe and the Rivonia Trial.
Explain Biko, SASO and Black Consciousness, and the Soweto uprising.
Explain international opposition: reaction to Sharpeville, the Anti-Apartheid Movement, UN divisions and the 1977 arms embargo.
Explain the OAU's support for the ANC and PAC.
Explain separate development under Verwoerd and Vorster and the growth of Bantustans.
Explain life in the Bantustans.
Explain the reaction to Sharpeville and Vorster's use of police and defence forces.
Explain the persecution of Biko and the government reaction to Soweto.

topics.title: 2.3 Why did apartheid and minority rule come to an end, 1978-94?

outcomes.text: Explain the problems facing Botha and his Total Strategy of reform and repression.
Explain de Klerk's reforms and the roles of de Klerk, Mandela and others.
Explain continuing violence: the Third Force, white extremists and Inkatha.
Explain the negotiations of 1992-93, the 1994 election and the new government.

topics.title: 2.4 How was the end of white minority rule in Zimbabwe achieved, 1965-80?

outcomes.text: Explain Rhodesia's demands for independence and the Wilson-Smith talks.
Explain UDI and the reactions in Rhodesia and Britain.
Explain the aims and methods of the Rhodesian government.
Describe ZAPU, ZIPRA and Nkomo, and ZANU, ZANLA and Mugabe, and the nature of the fighting.
Explain why Smith agreed to the Internal Settlement and the Muzorewa government.
Explain rejection by Britain, ZAPU and ZANU.
Explain why the fighting ended and the Lancaster House Agreement.
Explain the 1980 elections and Mugabe's government.

units.title: Paper 4: 3 The route to independence: Malaysia and Indonesia, c.1909-67

topics.title: 3.1 How widespread was nationalism and hostility to colonial rule in Malaya up to 1945?

outcomes.text: Explain why Britain gained protection of the Unfederated Malay States, including the Bangkok Treaty.
Explain divide and rule, immigration and Clementi's failed Malayanisation.
Explain the growth of nationalism: KMM, English-educated Malays, Kaum Muda and associations.
Explain Japanese treatment of the races and the Malayan Military Administration.
Explain the growth of resistance such as the MPAJA.
Explain how occupation grew nationalism, with the MPAJA, KMM, PETA and KRIS.

topics.title: 3.2 What factors led to the formation of Malaysia?

outcomes.text: Explain the failure of the Malayan Union and the role of Onn Jaafar and UMNO.
Explain the Federation of Malaya, 1948, and non-Malay opposition: PMCJA and PUTERA.
Explain the Emergency: Lai Teck, Chin Peng and the terror of 1948-49.
Explain Britain's response and success: the Briggs Plan and Templer.
Explain the growth of parties and the 1955 election: UMNO, MCA, MIC and the Alliance.
Explain the Reid Commission, Merdeka Constitution and Tunku Abdul Rahman's role.
Explain why Singapore merged with Malaya and why it later separated.

topics.title: 3.3 How did the nationalist movement develop in Indonesia up to 1945?

outcomes.text: Explain the Ethical Policy, Volksraad, Chinese trade, language, religion and westernised education.
Explain the nationalist parties PKI, PNI, Partindo, Gerindo and the Club Pendidikan.
Explain the leadership of Sukarno, Hatta and Sartono, the Soetardjo Petition and Gapi.
Explain Indonesia's role in the Co-Prosperity Sphere, conscription and administrative changes.
Explain the Triple A movement.
Explain Japan's methods to encourage nationalism: anti-western feeling, self-government promises, Putera and Peta.
Explain underground resistance.

topics.title: 3.4 What factors led to the formation of Indonesia and what challenges did it face?

outcomes.text: Explain the 1944 Preparatory Committee and the roles of Sukarno and Hatta.
Explain student protest and Sukarno's Pancasila.
Explain the Revolution: reactions to the 1945 declaration, the 1946 events, Linggadjati and UN and US involvement.
Explain 1950s political, economic and social challenges and Sukarno's leadership.
Explain Konfrontasi, the 30 September Movement and the purge of communists.
Explain KAMI protests and the Supersemar.
